title: Mitigating long-tail spikes: multipath KV, quantized inference, and on-prem topology - Ember Analytics
summary: Deep dive on p95/p99 spikes Ember is seeing in their on-prem setup. Discussed KV cache hot-shard behavior across multi-path network, tradeoffs between streaming vs non-streaming, quantization impacts on latency variance, and potential mitigations (routing policies, sticky cache shards, prefix caching, fallback model variants). Agreed to run a focused benchmark and share kernel-level profiling artifacts.
topics: KV cache hot shards and sharding strategy
next_steps: Redwood to share kernel-level profiling checklist and requested perf counters
Ember to run provided benchmark harness on three representative nodes and share logs
Schedule follow-up bench on Sep 8 2026 for results review
action_items: Evan Brooks: prepare perf-counter checklist and small tracing script by 2026-09-01
Tom Reynolds: run benchmark harness on stage cluster and upload logs by 2026-09-05
Maya Chen: send pricing / pilot contract template and security docs (SOC2 summary) by 2026-08-31
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-29 14:00 UTC | Duration 52m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Evan (Redwood SE), Luis (Redwood SE), Priya (CTO Ember), Tom (SRE), Hannah (ML Eng), Dave (Infra)

Summary: quick recap at top — Ember seeing intermittent p99 spikes in production for chat completions, particularly with 2-3 network hops to on-prem GPU clusters. Goal: identify root cause and immediate mitigations (routing, caching, quantization profiles) and agree bench plan.

[00:00] Maya Chen: okay hi everyone, thanks for carving time. quick intro, i'm Maya, i'm the AE on the account. evan and luis here are our solutions engineers. priya, do you want to kick off with what you're seeing?
[00:14] Priya Shah: yeah, thanks. so, quick context — we've got a mixed on-prem cluster behind our VPC edge, model is a 27B trimmed variant, quantized to 4-bit, and the p50 is fine, p95 also okay most days, but we get these p99 spikes where response latency jumps 3-5x for a small percent of requests. it's kinda unpredictable.
[00:36] Tom Reynolds: and to add, the spikes correlate with certain request patterns, specifically multi-turn chat where the token cache grows and we see more KV reads that fan out to multiple shards across nodes. sometimes it's also tied to an interconnect path where the edge chooses a different hop.
[00:55] Evan Brooks: okay, so two axis — KV hot-shard / fanout and network multipath variance. good. can you describe your sharding scheme? is it round robin at the proxy or hash-based on prefix?
[01:06] Tom Reynolds: today our proxy does simple consistent-hash by request id, but we left room for sticky session affinity. most of the time it balances but occasional keys create hot partitions.
[01:22] Hannah Kim: and one more nuance — we enabled a lossy quantization profile to hit cost SLA; i suspect quantize artifacts might make certain token expansions slower because kernel selection goes down a slower execution path.
[01:36] Luis Ortega: right, quantization can change kernel dispatch and trigger fallback slow paths, especially for attention or rotary ops if the kernel isn't optimized for 4-bit layout. also KV cache size and serialization overhead can amplify that if we serialize across network more often.
[01:52] Priya Shah: so, root cause might be interplay. we wanted to run with you through what you've seen at redwood in similar setups and what mitigations are effective.

[02:05] Evan Brooks: sure. quick runthrough of patterns we've observed: (1) hot-shard reads — when the prefix distribution is skewed you get queuing at the shard, (2) multipath network jitter — packets taking different routes cause reorders and added latency, (3) quantization fallback — poorly supported quant kernels create longer per-token times on a subset of sequences.
[02:28] Evan Brooks: mitigation surface: sticky routing for sessions, prefix caching at the edge, per-prefix hot-key replication, and adaptive batching that avoids batch growth for low-latency traces. also streaming vs non-streaming affects SLOs — streaming tends to surface latency earlier but can increase tail if network is lossy.
[02:47] Tom Reynolds: we actually use streaming for UX but we could flip to non-streaming for some routes as an experiment. what would be the tradeoffs?
[02:55] Evan Brooks: streaming lowers TTFIRSTBYTE for many requests but at p99 if packets drop or we hit a different node mid-session, you see bigger impact because of partial state and rerouting. non-streaming (buffered) gets you a single atomic request/response which can reduce variance but adds median latency.
[03:13] Hannah Kim: so is there a hybrid? start streaming until you detect a re-route/hot-shard then fallback to buffered?
[03:20] Luis Ortega: yeah that's exactly the streaming-fallback policy we recommend — monitor KV cache hit rate and network RTT, if you detect instability switch to non-streaming for that session or route. the runtime supports an automatic per-session policy.

[03:37] Priya Shah: what about quantization — we want 4-bit to save cost but not at the expense of tail. any profiling tips to know if quant is the culprit?
[03:47] Evan Brooks: run microbenchmarks: step through typical sequences with and without quant, capture per-layer time and kernel occupancy. look for bimodal distributions — if you see two clusters in per-token latency that's a sign of fallback kernels. also check CPU-side serialization times for KV RPCs — sometimes the extra CPU memcpy or python wrapper is the slow bit, not GPU.
[04:09] Tom Reynolds: we can share an example of logs. we saw these 200-500ms spikes in some tokens even though GPU utilization was flat.
[04:18] Luis Ortega: flat GPU util with spikes usually points to kernel contention or serialization/queueing on the host. or waiting on a remote KV read. can you check your per-node event latency and the time spent waiting on gRPC calls?

[04:35] Priya Shah: we use an internal RPC stack for KV reads; it's high throughput but not perfectly instrumented. would you recommend swapping to a more efficient binary bundle or change serialization?
[04:45] Evan Brooks: yes — reduce serialization overhead and prefer a compact binary proto. also ensure you use persistent connections with pipelining so you don't pay handshake costs. and co-locate small KV partitions with inference handlers when possible to avoid crossing the host boundary.

[05:02] Maya Chen: quick note on topology — you mentioned multi-hop. can you sketch the traffic path? edge LB -> firewall -> proxy -> on-prem inference nodes?
[05:12] Dave Li: that's it. sometimes traffic is also hairpinned through an auxiliary region for failover which adds an extra hop and we see those p99s cluster around those windows.
[05:23] Evan Brooks: hairpinning is a common affector. if stateful sessions get re-routed mid-conversation you lose KV locality. two mitigations: avoid hairpin except during maintenance windows; and maintain a lightweight session directory at the edge so you can quickly route back to the original shard.

[05:41] Priya Shah: okay can you go into sticky routing — is that just session affinity? how do you avoid hot-shard overload?
[05:48] Luis Ortega: sticky routing is session affinity plus active hot-key replication. when you identify a hot prefix, replicate that prefix's KV to 2-3 nearby shards proactively. that costs memory but reduces remote reads. we also throttle or shed low-priority requests during hot-shard events.
[06:05] Tom Reynolds: pelase elaborate on prefix caching — is this at the edge or per-node?
[06:10] Evan Brooks: edge prefix caching is often the best first line. cache recent KV entries at the LB/edge so short-lived conversational state doesn't hit the cluster. we also expose TTL and invalidation controls. with consistent hashing you'd still need to ensure cache consistency for writes — most teams choose read-heavy caching with write-through to the authoritative shard.

[06:30] [00:06:30] Hannah Kim: interruption — does Redwood support partial KV replication automatically or is that something we configure?
[06:36] Evan Brooks: currently we provide APIs and an operator that can manage replication rules; in Dedicated/Private deployments you can run the operator and set replication policies. for Hosted we manage it as a config. it's not magic auto-detect — you guide it with heatmaps / telemetry.

[06:52] [00:06:52] Priya Shah: let's talk about adaptive batching — you mentioned avoiding batch growth for low-latency traces. can you give an example policy?
[07:00] Luis Ortega: one policy is dynamic latency-aware batching: maintain a target p50 and p95; if predictors suggest a low-latency trace (small token counts, high priority), pin that trace to isolated worker lanes with smaller batch sizes; lower priority or bulk requests go through larger batch lanes. also set an absolute timeout cap so batches don't wait past X ms.
[07:20] Tom Reynolds: is that implemented in the runtime or at app layer?
[07:24] Evan Brooks: runtime. Redwood runtime supports lane isolation and priority decorators. you annotate requests with priority and max-wait and the runtime routes accordingly.

[07:35] [00:07:35] Priya Shah: this is helpful. can you walk us through the bench plan you recommend so our results are diagnostic?
[07:42] Evan Brooks: sure. we recommend three bench phases: (A) microbench per-layer with synthetic tokens to compare quant vs fp16; (B) end-to-end replay with production traces including multi-turn prefixes to measure p50/p95/p99; (C) fault-injection: simulate hairpin and node failover to see routing effects. collect per-token timing, gRPC latencies, kernel dispatch counts, and per-node queue lengths. we'll provide the harness and the perf counter checklist.
[08:10] Tom Reynolds: perfect. what perf counters do you want specifically?
[08:14] Luis Ortega: kernel exec time, kernel queue depth, memcpy times host->device, RPC roundtrip hist, KV lookup latency per shard, CPU syscalls causing stalls, swap/oom events (if any), NIC queue drops, and if possible, kernel selection path info (quant fallback flag).

[08:35] [00:08:35] Hannah Kim: about quant fallback flag — how do we see that? is it in the runtime logs?
[08:39] Evan Brooks: yes runtime emits a kernel path tag per op. in our logs you'll see entries like kernel_path=fast_int4 or kernel_path=fallback_fp32. those correlate strongly with per-token latency shifts.

[08:55] Priya Shah: ok, low-level question — we've had some confusion about streaming vs non-streaming implementation in our stack. are there gotchas for on-prem with flaky interconnects?
[09:03] Evan Brooks: main gotchas: streaming requires sustained reliable transport, so any packet reordering or transient disconnect magnifies tail because state is streamed incrementally. for on-prem with flaky interconnect use forwarding with retransmit and prefer TCP with appropriate congestion settings or gRPC keepalive tuning; add a session resume token so if streaming breaks you can resume without re-evaluating whole prefix.

[09:24] Tom Reynolds: is session resume supported out of box?
[09:27] Luis Ortega: yes, Redwood's runtime supports resumable streaming tokens for session continuation — you need to enable it and set a retention window for KV cache. retention is the knob — longer retention means higher memory but faster resume.

[09:43] [00:09:43] Maya Chen: are there short-term mitigations Ember can apply today before the bench? things you can flip that are low-risk?
[09:50] Priya Shah: we'd like that list.
[09:52] Evan Brooks: short list: 1) enable sticky session affinity for conversational routes (low risk), 2) enable edge prefix caching with small TTLs (30s-120s), 3) reduce aggressive quantization to hybrid fp16 for critical routes (config change), 4) add per-route streaming-fallback policy, 5) enable perf counters logging on a sample (1%) of requests to avoid noise.
[10:12] Tom Reynolds: we'll try 1 and 2 immediately and flip quant on one route to test.

[10:20] Priya Shah: one more question on testing: we'd like Redwood to run a short remote benchmark against a representative sample, is that possible with Private deployment?
[10:28] Evan Brooks: yes — for Private we can run a bench harness you host; we provide the binary and scripts and remote support. for Dedicated/Hosted we can run in our env but given on-prem constraints we'll ship the harness to you.

[10:40] [00:10:40] Hannah Kim: quick nit — what about persistent KV local caches vs in-memory eviction? if we persist on SSD, does that help tail?
[10:47] Luis Ortega: persisting helps cold-starts but SSD adds latency and variability; in-memory replication is best for tail especially for small KV entries. SSD is fallback for large state. also ensure your NIC and kernel tuning avoid interrupt coalescing spikes.

[10:58] Tom Reynolds: interrupt coalescing — we had some odd jitter there, we'll add NIC tuning to the bench plan.

[11:06] [00:11:06] Priya Shah: let's do a quick run of hypothetical numbers — if we enable sticky routing + edge caching what improvement might we expect on observed p99? ballpark?
[11:13] Evan Brooks: depends on skew — for moderate skew you can see p99 improvement of 30-60% for KV read-heavy traces. if hairpinning is the dominant cause you might see even larger gains. again bench will tell.

[11:25] Luis Ortega: also quant fallback remediation — moving to hybrid fp16 for critical tokens can shave off that bimodal cluster and reduce p99 by 20-40% depending on sequence shape.

[11:36] [00:11:36] Priya Shah: good. any long-term architecture suggestions beyond these immediate mitigations?
[11:41] Evan Brooks: long term: consider partition-aware placement (co-locate inference and its hot KV partitions), centralized session directory at the edge, smarter sharding (prefix-aware hashing), and invest in kernel-optimized quant kernels or use model variants that are quant-friendly. also continuous evals for tail — tie evals to real prompt sets so regressions surface early.

[12:04] Tom Reynolds: quick ask — are there known issues with specific NIC vendors or switches that trigger these tails? we've seen one vendor cause bursts under load.
[12:12] Luis Ortega: some older switches with shallow buffers can cause bursts; also NIC drivers with aggressive offloading modes can create micro-bursts. we recommend testing with NIC driver versions and turning off overly aggressive offloads during bench. we'll share a short checklist.

[12:28] [00:12:28] Priya Shah: Great, this is actionable. Maya, can you confirm deliverables and timeline?
[12:33] Maya Chen: yes. Evan will share perf-counter checklist and tracing script by Sept 1. I'll send SOC2 summary and pilot pricing by Aug 31. Tom will run the harness and upload logs by Sept 5. Follow-up meeting booked Sep 8 to review results.

[12:49] [00:12:49] Priya Shah: one small clarification — when you say "prefix caching TTL 30s-120s" what's the default recommended?
[12:56] Evan Brooks: start with 60s and tune based on observed hit-rate and write frequency. if you have high-turn writes shorten TTL.

[13:05] [00:13:05] Hannah Kim: can we get an example of the runtime log snippet that contains the kernel_path tag? would help our ops team parse it.
[13:11] Evan Brooks: yes we'll include sample log lines in the checklist — e.g., kernel_path=fast_int4 kernel_id=0x3f exec_ms=1.2.

[13:20] Tom Reynolds: any precautions for running bench under prod-like traffic? we don't want to destabilize infra.
[13:25] Luis Ortega: run bench on stage, or run a small mirrored sample of traffic at <10% to avoid overload. prioritize sampling of critical routes. and enable circuit-breakers.

[13:36] [00:13:36] Priya Shah: ok last question — are there toolings Redwood provides for visualizing per-token latency clusters?
[13:42] Evan Brooks: yes, Redwood Console has a per-token waterfall and kernel-path heatmap; we'll give you access to a demo tenant and a small workbook that maps kernel_path to latency clusters.

[13:56] Maya Chen: great. thanks everyone. we'll recap and send artifacts. any final thoughts?
[14:02] Hannah Kim: no, this was productive. thanks.
[14:05] Priya Shah: thanks all.

Meeting close at 14:52 UTC.

Notes on transcription: occasional filler words left in, speaker labels approximate, some technical terms may be slightly transcribed (K-V vs KV, quantize vs quantization), logs and artifact names abbreviated.
